rv.q: Whether you were there, in situ or on sofa, first time round or not, be prepared for a smile on your lips, a tear in your eyes and a lingering itch to do good.
Just For One Day absolutely nuking, erasing and laying waste to all cynicism — to ensure Saint Bob and crew rise again.
You'd need a heart of stone not to tap a toe to these old bangers and not be moved by this huge collective effort to do some good in the world.
Director Luke Sheppard marshals, with considerable style, a huge cast of 25, plus an on-stage band of six, whose combined talents make an utterly joyous noise.
Just for One Day remains an excuse for some great tunes and boasts a fantastic ensemble, tightly directed by Luke Sheppard.
But as drama it struggles, weighed down by trying to outline the history and emphasise its current relevance.
It’s unsubtle and overlong, but it’s determined to show you a great time.
In the end, this celebration of Live Aid is a bit like that long-ago day itself — long, uneven and sometimes gauche, but redeemed by uplifting anthems and a spirit of positivity.

Ultimately your love of ‘Just for One Day’ will almost certainly rest on your fondness for the original songs and Matthew Brind’s modernised musical arrangements of them: think more soul, more sincerity.
Despite the relentless insistence on showing us a good time, I couldn't shake the feeling that we'd been fed a slightly hollow platitude.
But somehow this show states these criticisms without giving them any actual weight, like a bad boyfriend glibly listing his failings in a voicenote plea for reconciliation.
But where is the story, surprise, character study and ethical debate on such celebrity endorsed acts of “charidy”?
I was left ice-cold by its overlong mixture of the earnest, the cheesily comical and the anthemic.
It’s also a blisteringly good time, thanks to one of the best back catalogues available to any jukebox musical.
The musical is also an electric beacon of hope that reverberates long into the night.
At the end of it all – it’s not hard to imagine this charming the pants off a mainstream theatregoing audience – with tunes to delight and a cockle-warming account of a vastly successful occasion.
With a mixture of nostalgia and a consideration of how much logistical effort was required to pull off Live Aid, it’s a very slick and brilliantly performed production.
That's symbolic of this boisterously played but problematic musical about Live Aid/Band Aid: tremendous musical performances, shame about the book.
The writer, John O’Farrell, captures Geldof brilliantly in a complex and unsympathetic portrait of a prickly yob.
The gesture was important but didn’t deal with the problem.

The narrative really sparks when O’Farrell leaves behind the need to explain and justify and simply goes for the funny bone, attacking his old bête noir, Mrs Thatcher (a show-stealing Julie Atherton).
While the script may be full of exposition and awkward phrasing, the music is brilliant and saves this production from complete failure.
In terms of reminding us all why Live Aid mattered, Just For One Day is one of the most important musicals on stage right now.
As a celebration and reminder of what human beings can achieve when moved by compassion it is a triumph.
It was clearly enraptured – this production, directed by Luke Sheppard, is going to be a hit with the public, if not with the critics – but at first, I couldn’t quite work out why.
And yet, you just can’t stop coming back to the idea that staging a celebratory show about an out-of-date movement given the current political climate feels utterly tone deaf.
It makes for a great night out that’s as exhilarating and moving as Live Aid itself.

cn.t: Critics find this Live Aid musical energetic and well-performed but dramatically thin, with a clunky book that leans heavily on nostalgia and hagiography. The stellar song catalog and spirited cast elevate uneven material that skirts ethical debate.
